MATH 105-8 First-Year Writing Seminar (1 Unit) Small, writing and discussion-oriented course exploring a specific topic or theme, and focused on the fundamentals of effective, college-level written communication. Not eligible to be applied towards a WCAS major or minor except where specifically indicated.

Title: Mathematics in the Cultural Imagination

Description: What do we imagine when we think of mathematics, and how does that compare with the experiences of those who practice it? Mathematics has been celebrated as a source of beauty, truth, and progress, while simultaneously being seen as inaccessible, intimidating, and useless. Where do these perceptions come from, and how do they shape its place in society?

This seminar explores the interplay between mathematical culture and the wider world. We will consider what mathematical work involves, how mathematics influences society, how the surrounding culture shapes developments in mathematics, and how public perceptions of mathematics compare with the experiences of mathematicians. Class meetings will center on discussion of the readings, providing opportunities to examine authors' arguments and develop our own responses.

This course has no mathematics prerequisites. Rather than studying mathematics directly, we will focus on a skill essential both within and beyond mathematics: communicating ideas clearly through writing.

Title: The Distribution of Primes

Prime numbers appear irregularly distributed among the integers, yet collectively they obey remarkably precise asymptotic laws. This seminar surveys analytic and sieve methods for studying the primes. We will familiarize ourselves with some classical results, such as the Prime Number Theorem and its connection to the Riemann Hypothesis and get a glimpse of combinatorial tools behind modern work on primes in intervals and twin primes. Students will present selected topics, and those with a more advanced background will have the opportunity to explore special topics, if desired.

The study of prime numbers connects many areas of mathematics, including real analysis, complex analysis, harmonic analysis, combinatorics, and probability theory. The course assumes no knowledge beyond basic real analysis.

Prerequisite: Math 320-1 and experience with proofs, or instructor's permission.
